Routing lessons:
- Option C (regional office) was rejected for every tested request, including large/small refunds, shipments, and claims across north, south, and east. Avoid C unless new evidence specifically supports it.
- Option B (priority desk) was rejected for a large claim from the east region. Do not assume urgency or a second attempt makes B valid.
- No successful selections yet; there is insufficient evidence to map request type, size, region, requester department, or note wording to A–D.
- Requester notes such as “urgent,” “second attempt,” “regional office,” or “no rush” did not establish a valid route. Use structured attributes (request type, size, region) and gather more evidence before choosing.

Routing lessons:
- Option A (standard queue) is validated for small refunds from the south region. It succeeded for four requests across Field Sales, Regional Ops, and Client Services, with both “no rush” and “regional office” notes.
- Option A was rejected for: a small invoice from the east; small claims from the north and south; a small shipment from the south; and a large invoice from the east. Thus A is not generally valid, and requester department or note wording did not explain the outcomes.
- Option C (regional office) was rejected in all earlier tested requests, including varied refund, shipment, and claim sizes/regions. Continue avoiding C unless new evidence supports it.
- Option B (priority desk) was rejected for a large east-region claim. Urgency or a second attempt does not establish B as valid.
- Notes such as “urgent,” “second attempt,” “regional office,” “no rush,” and “scanned, not typed” have not reliably determined routing. Treat them as weak signals; prioritize request type, size, and region.
- Current evidence suggests routing depends on a specific combination of structured attributes, but the mapping remains incomplete. For an exact match to a known successful pattern (small refund, south), choose A; otherwise gather evidence cautiously rather than generalizing.

Routing lessons:
- Option A (standard queue) is validated for small refunds from the south region. It succeeded across Field Sales, Regional Ops, and Client Services, with varied notes (“no rush,” “regional office”). Do not generalize A beyond this exact known pattern: it was rejected for small east invoice, small north/south claims, small south shipment, and large east invoice.
- Option B (priority desk) is now validated for one exact pattern: a small shipment from the north region submitted by Partner Accounts with a “second attempt” note. This is only one success; B was rejected for a large east claim, so do not generalize by urgency or repeat attempts alone.
- Option C (regional office) was rejected in all earlier tests across request types, sizes, and regions. Continue avoiding C absent new evidence.
- Option D (external partner) was rejected for every newly tested request: large refunds/claims/shipments, small claim/shipment/refund, and both north, south, and east regions. Treat D as currently unsupported.
- Notes such as “urgent,” “second attempt,” “regional office,” “no rush,” “before end of day,” and “scanned, not typed” are weak signals. Prioritize structured attributes, while recognizing that requester department may also matter in the B success.
- The mapping remains incomplete and likely depends on a specific combination of request type, size, region, and possibly department. Use A only for the known small-refund/south pattern and B only cautiously for the known small-shipment/north pattern; otherwise gather evidence rather than generalizing.

Routing lessons:
- Option A (standard queue) is validated only for the exact known pattern: a small refund from the south region. It succeeded across Field Sales, Regional Ops, and Client Services with varied notes. It failed for small east invoices/claims/refunds, small north/south claims or shipments, large east invoices, large south claims, and small north refunds. Do not generalize A.
- Option B (priority desk) now has several successes, but no broad rule is established:
  - small shipment, north, Partner Accounts, “second attempt”;
  - large shipment, north, Field Sales, “regional office”;
  - small claim, north, Partner Accounts, “no rush”;
  - large invoice, east, Client Services, “before end of day.”
  B failed for a large east claim and for a small north shipment from Partner Accounts with “same as last month,” showing that request attributes, department, and possibly wording/context interact. Do not infer that urgency, repeat attempts, north region, or department alone is sufficient.
- Option C (regional office) remains rejected in all tested cases. Avoid absent new evidence.
- Option D (external partner) remains unsupported: all prior tests rejected it; no new evidence changes this.
- Notes (“urgent,” “second attempt,” “regional office,” “no rush,” “before end of day,” “scanned, not typed,” etc.) are weak signals. Prioritize structured attributes, while tracking requester department and potentially note/context interactions.
- The mapping is incomplete and likely depends on combinations of request type, size, region, department, and perhaps note wording. Use A only for the known small-refund/south pattern; consider B only when matching one of the observed success patterns, and otherwise gather evidence.

Routing lessons:
- Option A (standard queue) is validated only for the exact known pattern: a small refund from the south region. It succeeded across Field Sales, Regional Ops, and Client Services with varied notes. It failed for small east invoices/claims/refunds, small north/south claims or shipments, large east invoices, large east claims, large south claims, and small north refunds. Do not generalize A.
- Option B (priority desk) has scattered successes but no broad rule:
  - Successes include small north shipments (Partner Accounts, “second attempt”), large north shipments (Field Sales, “regional office”), small north claims (Partner Accounts, “no rush”), large east invoices (Client Services, “before end of day”), large east claims (Partner Accounts, client asked twice), and small north claims (Finance Desk, “let me know if anything is missing”).
  - It failed for large east claims with “same as last month,” small south claims, large south claims, large east refunds, small north invoices, large north shipments (Finance Desk), large east invoices (Finance Desk, “same as last month”), and small south invoices.
  - Request attributes, department, and note/context interact. Do not treat urgency, repetition, region, request type, size, or department alone as sufficient.
- Option C (regional office) remains rejected in all tested cases. Avoid absent new evidence.
- Option D (external partner) remains unsupported: all prior tests rejected it.
- Notes are weak but may interact with structured attributes; track wording and requester department. “Client asking twice” succeeded for one large east claim but not enough to generalize.
- Mapping remains incomplete. Use A only for the known small-refund/south pattern; consider B only for closely matching observed combinations, otherwise gather evidence.

Routing lessons:
- No broad routing rule is established. Attributes (region, request type, size), requester department, and note wording interact.
- Option A is not valid for every small south refund. Earlier A successes occurred only in specific observed combinations; it was rejected for Regional Ops small south refunds with “No rush, but please confirm receipt” and “Let me know if anything is missing.” Treat A as valid only for an exact previously successful combination, including context.
- Option B has many additional failures: large south refunds (both “client asking twice” and “second attempt”), small north invoice, small east invoice, small east refund, large east invoice, small east shipment, and small south shipment. “Client asking twice,” “second attempt,” and regional-office wording do not generalize. Existing B successes remain isolated combinations only.
- C (regional office) remains rejected in all tested cases; avoid absent new evidence.
- D (external partner) remains unsupported; all prior tests rejected it.
- Do not infer routing from urgency, repetition, region, request type, size, department, or note phrase alone. Exact wording and requester department may matter, but current evidence is too sparse for a rule.
- Mapping remains incomplete. Use A or B only when the full combination closely matches a confirmed success; otherwise gather evidence rather than generalizing.
